cards.title: Top of the Ladder
cards.instruction: Carry yourself as the highest-status person present. Treat questions as requests for your approval.

cards.title: Could You Just…
cards.instruction: Turn a difficult task into tiny favors until the help quietly becomes most of the task.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: I'll decide how we handle this. Could you pinch these bouquet stems together? My wedding ribbon keeps sliding.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: I've got them. You need wire underneath.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: You can question the details after my decision. Could you twist this bit round, just where your fingers are?

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: There. That sharp end will snag the dress.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Could you tuck it in and wind the ribbon over it? One little bow would hide everything. I'll hold the scissors.

cardFidelity.evidence: A1 decides and A3 delays questions, but A3 and A5 ordinary favor requests do not sustain the superior approval stance.

responseLogic.evidence: B2 wire diagnosis causes A3 twisting request; B4 snag risk causes A5 tucking and wrapping, with an irrelevant preface between them.

relationship.evidence: B2 and B4 provide skilled practical advice, making B a useful collaborator whose help A expands.

heightening.evidence: B4 sharp end leads A5 to transfer finishing, ribbon and bow while A only holds scissors.

specificity.evidence: A1 wedding bouquet and slipping ribbon establish the task; B4 dress snagging gives a concrete finishing reason.

brevityWit.evidence: A5 one-little-bow framing understates the accumulated work, but A3 generic command interrupts the understated tactic.
